Some answers require previous answer to a question on procedural quality. Why not make a combined procedural-reporting quality assessment, where the procedural element is valued right before the reporting element. E.g. 2 (simplified) questions would be:
-Did the authors adequately conduct a test of publication bias?
-Did the authors adequately report the test of publication bias?

The tool should be simple. For example, the first three questions should be consolidated into 1 and I'm not even sure they are that relevant to bias. There should also be if possible a test of whether these are true bias domains.

Don't be too dogmatic about meta-analysis. Encouraging better reporting is good but meta-analyses are broader than we often give it credit for. I think there's a lot of issue with that in the meta-analysis literature. For example, many folks fixate on effect sizes but there's often more ways to analyse data than just through an effect size (and the effect size might harm the analysis in some cases, or just make it less impactful). Dogma leads to formulaic meta-analyses which stifle scientific creativity and critical thinking and which often fail to really progress the science.
Best of luck with this endeavour. If this can be a bit more applicable to the environmental sciences than other tools like PRISMA, then I can see this getting adopted fairly easily, which will be a great benefit to the field of evidence synthesis.

I think the questions would greatly benefit from more thorough descriptions and examples. Some of the questions require some prior knowledge of meta-analysis and hence can be prone to errors for people not familiar with certain concepts. Precisely defining each term and giving examples of what is expected would make the tool less susceptible to biases and more standardized across authors.

It may bias results or show undue prestige for certain software/packages/stats, but it may be useful to provide examples in some of the questions, e.g., "R programming language", "metafor package", "I2 statistic".
This is a great initiative considering the absence of a comprehensive reporting quality appraisal tool for environmental sciences.
